By Sahil Rajesh Warke

The Question After the Rain

(The rain had just stopped. Cool air drifted through the college corridors as students hurried across the campus, careful not to step into the puddles that reflected the gray evening sky. Most classrooms had already emptied, leaving behind only the faint sounds of distant conversations and footsteps.

Professor Vinay closed the psychology textbook in his hands and slipped it into his leather bag. Just as he turned toward the corridor, he noticed someone standing a few feet away.

It was Rudhika.

She clutched her notebook tightly against her chest. Her eyes followed the professor for a moment before she gathered enough courage to speak.)

Rudhika: Professor… may I ask you something?

(Vinay looked up and smiled. He had begun to expect this. Whenever a lecture ended, Rudhika often seemed to leave with more questions than answers.)

Professor Vinay: (Closing the zipper of his bag.) You usually do.

(Rudhika let out a small, nervous smile. She lowered her eyes for a brief moment, wondering if her question would sound strange.)

Rudhika: Why do people fear questions?

(Vinay looked at her for a moment. Instead of answering immediately, he glanced around the nearly empty corridor.)

Professor Vinay: Before I answer… tell me something.

Rudhika: (Blinking in surprise.) Me?

Professor Vinay: Yes. You asked the question. So what do you think?

(Rudhika looked down at the wet floor. Tiny ripples danced in a puddle where raindrops still fell from the roof. She remained silent for a few seconds.)

Rudhika: (Thinking carefully.) Maybe… because questions expose what we don’t know.

Professor Vinay: Hmm.

Rudhika: (Gaining a little confidence.) If someone asks me something I can’t answer… I feel embarrassed. Maybe everyone feels that way.

Professor Vinay: That’s one possibility.

(He began walking slowly down the corridor. Rudhika followed a step behind, matching his pace.)

Professor Vinay: Let me ask you another question.

Rudhika: (Smiling faintly.) You always answer my questions with more questions.

Professor Vinay: (Chuckling.) Occupational hazard.

(Rudhika laughed softly.)

Professor Vinay: When you were a child, did you ask many questions?

Rudhika: Too many, according to my parents.

Professor Vinay: Were you afraid then?

Rudhika: No… not at all.

Professor Vinay: So something changed.

(Rudhika’s smile faded as she thought about it.)

Professor Vinay: A four-year-old can ask, “Why is the sky blue?” without worrying about sounding foolish. An adult often knows the question… but keeps it locked inside.

Rudhika: Why?

Professor Vinay: Because somewhere along the way, many of us begin believing that asking a question is the same as admitting ignorance.

(They walked in silence for a few moments. The sound of their footsteps echoed through the corridor.)

Professor Vinay: But think carefully, Rudhika. Which person remains ignorant the one who asks, or the one who stays silent because they’re afraid?

(Rudhika stopped walking.)

She didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, she watched a group of students pass by. They laughed loudly, discussing an upcoming assignment. One of them confidently explained a topic that, from what she had heard in class, was completely wrong.

She wondered how many people spoke confidently simply because they were afraid to ask.

Rudhika: (Quietly.) The one who stays silent…

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Knowledge rarely begins with an answer.

It almost always begins with the courage to ask a question.

(A gentle breeze drifted through the corridor, carrying the scent of rain-soaked earth. Most of the students had already left. The campus, which had been bustling only a few minutes ago, was slowly settling into silence.)

(Rudhika remained thoughtful. Vinay noticed she wasn’t completely convinced.)

Professor Vinay: Tell me honestly.

Rudhika: (Looking up.) Hmm?

Professor Vinay: Have you ever stopped yourself from asking a question?

(Rudhika let out a quiet laugh.)

Rudhika: More times than I can count.

Professor Vinay: Why?

Rudhika: (She hesitated.) Sometimes… I feel everyone else already understands. If I’m the only one asking, maybe they’ll think I’m slow.

Professor Vinay: Has anyone ever actually told you that?

Rudhika: No…

Professor Vinay: Then who told you?

(Rudhika opened her mouth to answer but stopped.)

(The question lingered in the air.)

Rudhika: (Softly.) I… don’t know.

Professor Vinay: Interesting, isn’t it?

(He rested one hand on the corridor railing.)

Professor Vinay: Sometimes the loudest critic in our lives isn’t another person.

It’s the voice we’ve built inside our own minds.

(Rudhika looked at him quietly.)

Professor Vinay: Psychology has a name for this.

Rudhika: (Her curiosity immediately returned.) It does?

Professor Vinay: We often create an imaginary audience.

We feel as though everyone is constantly watching us… judging every word we speak, every mistake we make.

But here’s something fascinating.

Most people are too busy worrying about themselves to spend much time thinking about you.

(Rudhika blinked.)

Rudhika: So… everyone is busy wondering what everyone else thinks of them?

Professor Vinay: (Smiling.) Exactly.

Imagine twenty students sitting in a classroom.

Nineteen of them are thinking,

“I hope nobody notices I’m confused.”

And the twentieth stays silent because she believes the other nineteen understand perfectly.

(Rudhika couldn’t help smiling.)

Rudhika: That… actually sounds like my classroom.

Professor Vinay: More classrooms than you might imagine.

(They resumed walking toward the college garden. Rainwater still clung to the leaves, sparkling in the fading evening light.)

Professor Vinay: Let me ask you one last question before we go home.

Rudhika: (Grinning slightly.) Another one?

Professor Vinay: Naturally.

If a question exists only inside your mind…

and you never ask it…

who loses more?

The teacher…

or you?

(Rudhika didn’t answer immediately.)

She imagined every question she had swallowed over the years.

Questions she thought were childish.

Questions she feared would make others laugh.

Questions that had quietly disappeared before they were ever spoken.

She looked at Professor Vinay.

Rudhika: I do.

Professor Vinay: (Nodding gently.) Exactly.

A teacher may lose one opportunity to explain.

But a student can lose years of understanding.

For a moment, neither of them spoke.

The silence no longer felt awkward.

It felt… thoughtful.

(The evening sun briefly peeked through the clouds, casting a soft golden light across the rain-washed campus. The puddles that had mirrored gray skies now reflected streaks of orange.)

(Rudhika and Professor Vinay continued walking toward the college garden. The silence between them was comfortable.)

Rudhika: Professor…

Professor Vinay: Hmm?

Rudhika: Were you always like this?

Professor Vinay: Like what?

Rudhika: Confident. Calm. The kind of person who never seems afraid to speak.

(Vinay smiled quietly, then looked ahead instead of at her.)

Professor Vinay: Not even close.

(Rudhika looked surprised.)

Rudhika: Really?

Professor Vinay: When I was in my first year of college, I was sitting exactly where you usually sit.

The third bench.

Near the window.

(Rudhika listened intently.)

Professor Vinay: One day, my professor was teaching memory.

He said something that didn’t make sense to me.

I thought about raising my hand…

I even lifted it halfway.

(He paused.)

Professor Vinay: Then I looked around.

Everyone else was writing notes.

No one seemed confused.

So I told myself, “The problem must be me.”

I lowered my hand.

Rudhika: (Quietly.) What happened then?

Professor Vinay: Nothing.

That’s the problem.

Nothing happened.

The class ended.

Life moved on.

But my question stayed with me.

For weeks.

(Rudhika frowned.)

Rudhika: You never asked it?

Professor Vinay: No.

I convinced myself it wasn’t important.

Months later, while reading a psychology book, I found the answer by accident.

Do you know what shocked me?

(Rudhika shook her head.)

Professor Vinay: My confusion had been completely reasonable.

The professor had skipped an important explanation.

Several students had misunderstood the topic.

Nobody asked.

Everybody assumed everyone else understood.

(Rudhika lowered her eyes.)

Rudhika: So… everyone was pretending.

Professor Vinay: Not pretending.

Protecting their image.

There’s a difference.

People often protect how intelligent they appear…

even if it costs them becoming more intelligent.

(The words settled heavily in Rudhika’s mind.)

Rudhika: (After a long pause.) Professor…

Professor Vinay: Yes?

Rudhika: Have you ever been asked a question you couldn’t answer?

(Vinay laughed.)

Not a small laugh.

A genuine, wholehearted laugh.

A few nearby pigeons fluttered into the air.

Professor Vinay: Almost every year.

(Rudhika stared at him.)

Rudhika: Seriously?

Professor Vinay: Of course.

Do you know what I tell my students?

Rudhika: What?

Professor Vinay: “I don’t know.”

(Rudhika blinked in disbelief.)

Professor Vinay: Then I add…

“Let’s find out together.”

Knowledge isn’t damaged by admitting ignorance.

It’s strengthened by the willingness to explore it.

(Rudhika smiled.

For the first time since the conversation began, she felt that asking questions wasn’t a test she had to pass.

It was an invitation to think.)

Just then, the college bell rang in the distance.

The campus was officially closing for the day.

(The bell echoed through the campus one last time. A security guard in the distance began locking the classrooms.)

Professor Vinay: I suppose that’s our signal to leave.

(Rudhika nodded and adjusted the strap of her bag. They walked toward the college gate at an unhurried pace.)

After a few moments, Vinay spoke again.

Professor Vinay: Rudhika.

Rudhika: Yes, Professor?

Professor Vinay: Can I tell you something I’ve noticed about you?

(Rudhika looked slightly nervous.)

Rudhika: Is… is something wrong?

Professor Vinay: Quite the opposite.

(He smiled.)

Professor Vinay: In every class, there are students who ask questions because they want to impress others.

There are students who ask questions because they’re preparing for an examination.

And then…

there are a very few students who ask questions because they genuinely want to understand.

(He looked at her.)

Professor Vinay: You’re one of them.

(Rudhika froze for a moment.)

She wasn’t expecting that.

A faint warmth spread across her cheeks.

She quickly looked away, pretending to straighten the notebook she was already holding perfectly.

Rudhika: (Embarrassed.) I… I just ask whatever comes to my mind.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Never lose that.

Facts can be memorized.

Curiosity cannot.

(It was one of the simplest compliments Rudhika had ever received.

Yet somehow…

it felt like one of the most meaningful.)

(They reached the college gate. Outside, the roads still glistened from the rain.)

Rudhika: Professor…

Professor Vinay: Hmm?

Rudhika: Can I ask… one last question?

(Vinay laughed softly.)

Professor Vinay: I was wondering how long it would take.

(Rudhika smiled.)

Rudhika: If asking questions is so important…

then why do some people become angry when their own beliefs are questioned?

(Vinay’s smile remained, but this time there was a thoughtful look in his eyes.)

He glanced at the darkening sky and then at his watch.

Professor Vinay: That’s not a five-minute conversation.

(Rudhika looked slightly disappointed.)

Professor Vinay: Tomorrow.

Same time.

After class.

We’ll talk about why people defend beliefs as if they’re defending themselves.

(Rudhika nodded eagerly.)

Professor Vinay: Until then…

I want you to observe something.

Don’t argue with anyone.

Don’t try to change anyone’s mind.

Just notice how people react when someone politely questions an opinion.

You might discover more than any textbook could teach you.

(Rudhika smiled.)

Rudhika: Homework?

Professor Vinay: (Grinning.) Psychology homework.

(The professor walked toward the faculty parking area.

Rudhika stood at the gate for a few moments, watching him disappear into the evening.

Then she looked up at the clearing sky.

Tomorrow suddenly felt much closer than it had a minute ago.)

End of Chapter 1

The Weight of Belief

(The next afternoon, the Psychology lecture ended as usual. Students packed their bags while conversations quickly filled the classroom.

Rudhika remained seated.

She wasn’t writing notes.

Instead, she was thinking about yesterday’s homework.

She had spent the entire evening quietly observing people.

On the bus to college, two strangers argued over politics.

Neither seemed interested in understanding the other.

Both wanted to win.

Even in the college canteen that morning, she had watched two classmates debate whether artificial intelligence would replace teachers. Within minutes, the discussion had turned personal.

It wasn’t about ideas anymore.

It was about proving who was right.

(The final bell rang.)

Students slowly left the classroom.

Professor Vinay closed his attendance register and smiled as he noticed Rudhika waiting patiently near the front desk.)

Professor Vinay: (Picking up his notebook.) I see someone has completed her homework.

Rudhika: (Smiling shyly.) I think so.

Professor Vinay: “Think so?”

Rudhika: I noticed something… but I’m not sure if I understood it correctly.

Professor Vinay: That’s the best kind of observation.

(They stepped out of the classroom together.

The weather was completely different from yesterday.

The rain had disappeared, leaving behind a bright blue sky and a gentle afternoon breeze.

As they walked toward the college garden, Rudhika opened her notebook.

Several pages were filled with small observations.

Vinay glanced at them and raised an eyebrow.)

Professor Vinay: You took notes?

Rudhika: (Embarrassed.) I didn’t want to forget anything.

Professor Vinay: (Smiling.) Psychology begins with observation.

So…

What did you discover?

(Rudhika took a slow breath.)

Rudhika: I think…

people don’t actually argue because they want the truth.

They argue because they want to be right.

(Vinay didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, he looked at the trees lining the garden path. A gentle breeze rustled the leaves, and for a few moments, the only sound between them was the chirping of birds.)

Professor Vinay: That’s an interesting observation.

(Rudhika waited quietly.)

Professor Vinay: Now tell me something.

Do you always want the truth?

(Rudhika looked confused.)

Rudhika: Of course.

Professor Vinay: Always?

Rudhika: (She thought for a moment.) I… I think so.

Professor Vinay: Good.

Let’s test that.

(He sat down on a wooden bench beneath a large banyan tree and gestured for Rudhika to sit beside him.)

Professor Vinay: Imagine you’ve spent an entire week preparing a presentation.

You work hard.

You practice every night.

You’re proud of it.

Then, just before you present, one of your classmates points out a mistake you’ve made.

How would you feel?

(Rudhika answered almost instantly.)

Rudhika: Embarrassed.

Professor Vinay: Why?

Rudhika: Because everyone would know I was wrong.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Notice something.

The mistake existed before your classmate mentioned it.

But it only began to hurt after someone exposed it.

(Rudhika’s expression slowly changed.)

Professor Vinay: So was the pain caused by the mistake…

or by the fact that your image of yourself was challenged?

(Rudhika remained silent.)

She replayed the situation in her mind.

If she had discovered the mistake herself at home, she would have simply corrected it.

But if someone pointed it out in front of everyone…

it felt different.

Much different.

Rudhika: (Quietly.) My image…

Professor Vinay: Good.

Now we’re getting somewhere.

(He smiled, not because she had given the correct answer, but because she had genuinely thought about it.)

Professor Vinay: Most arguments aren’t battles between ideas.

They’re battles between identities.

(Rudhika frowned.)

Rudhika: Identities?

Professor Vinay: Tell me…

if I say,

“The sky is blue,”

and you disagree…

would you be offended?

Rudhika: Probably not.

Professor Vinay: Why not?

Rudhika: Because… it doesn’t really matter to me.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Now imagine I insult someone you deeply admire.

Or criticize a belief you’ve held since childhood.

Would your reaction be the same?

(Rudhika instinctively shook her head.)

Professor Vinay: Why?

(Rudhika searched for the answer.)

Rudhika: Because…

it would feel personal.

Professor Vinay: There it is.

(He gently tapped the notebook resting on her lap.)

Professor Vinay: The moment an idea becomes part of our identity…

questioning the idea begins to feel like questioning us.

That’s why calm discussions suddenly become emotional.

People think they’re defending an opinion.

Often…

they’re defending themselves.

(Rudhika looked down at her notebook.)

She slowly wrote a single sentence.

“When beliefs become identity, disagreement feels like an attack.”

(Vinay noticed what she had written and smiled.)

Professor Vinay: That’s a sentence worth remembering.

(Rudhika looked up.)

Rudhika: Professor…

does that mean we should never become attached to our beliefs?

(Vinay’s smile grew slightly.)

Professor Vinay: Ah…

Now that’s a dangerous question.

(The corners of Rudhika’s lips curled into a small smile.)

She had begun to recognize that whenever Professor Vinay called a question “dangerous,” it usually led to one of his most interesting conversations.)

(Vinay leaned back against the bench, watching a few students walk across the garden. Two of them were discussing an assignment, each insisting their solution was correct.)

Professor Vinay: Before I answer your question…

look over there.

(Rudhika followed his gaze.)

Two students had stopped near the pathway.

One pointed repeatedly at a notebook while the other shook his head.

Neither seemed willing to listen.

Professor Vinay: What do you think they’re trying to do?

Rudhika: Convince each other.

Professor Vinay: Are they?

(Rudhika watched for another few seconds.)

One student interrupted before the other could finish speaking.

The second immediately interrupted back.

Neither paused to consider what the other was saying.

Rudhika: (Smiling faintly.) No…

They aren’t listening at all.

Professor Vinay: Then why are they talking?

(Rudhika folded her arms.)

Rudhika: To prove they’re right.

Professor Vinay: Good.

Now tell me…

if one of them suddenly realizes he’s wrong…

what’s the easiest thing to do?

Rudhika: Admit it.

Professor Vinay: (Grinning.) That’s the wisest thing to do.

I asked for the easiest.

(Rudhika thought again.)

Rudhika: …

Pretend the other person is wrong?

Professor Vinay: Better.

Anything easier?

(She frowned.)

Professor Vinay: Blame.

Change the topic.

Attack the person.

Ignore the evidence.

Walk away.

There are countless ways to protect an opinion.

There’s only one way to correct it.

(Rudhika slowly nodded.)

Professor Vinay: Our minds are remarkable.

They don’t simply search for truth.

Very often…

they search for comfort.

(The sentence lingered.)

Rudhika: Comfort?

Professor Vinay: Imagine someone has believed something for twenty years.

Now imagine you prove, beyond any doubt, that it’s false.

What have you taken away from them?

Rudhika: Their belief.

Professor Vinay: Only that?

(Rudhika hesitated.)

Professor Vinay: Perhaps you’ve also taken away years of certainty.

Perhaps memories connected to that belief.

Perhaps the feeling that they understood the world.

Sometimes…

people aren’t defending an idea.

They’re defending the world that idea helped them build.

(Rudhika remained quiet.)

She had never thought of beliefs that way.

Professor Vinay: That’s why changing someone’s mind is rarely an intellectual event.

It’s often an emotional one.

(A gentle silence settled between them.)

Rudhika looked down at the sentence she had written earlier.

“When beliefs become identity, disagreement feels like an attack.”

She underlined it.

Then she looked up.

Rudhika: Professor…

Have you ever changed one of your own deeply held beliefs?

(Vinay didn’t answer immediately.)

Instead…

he smiled.

Not because the question was easy.

But because it reminded him of a younger version of himself.

Professor Vinay: Yes.

And it was one of the most uncomfortable experiences of my life.

(Rudhika leaned forward with genuine curiosity.)

Rudhika: What happened?

(Vinay looked toward the old psychology building across the garden.)

Professor Vinay: That…

is a story worth telling.

(Vinay rested both hands on the walking stick beside the bench. His eyes remained fixed on the old psychology building.)

Professor Vinay: When I was in my second year of college…

I believed something with absolute confidence.

Not because I had examined it carefully.

But because everyone around me believed it.

(Rudhika listened quietly.)

Professor Vinay: One afternoon, I was discussing it with one of my professors.

I was convinced I was right.

I spoke with confidence.

I quoted books.

I even thought I had won the argument.

Rudhika: What did your professor say?

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: Almost nothing.

(Rudhika looked puzzled.)

Professor Vinay: He didn’t tell me I was wrong.

He didn’t laugh at me.

He didn’t embarrass me.

He simply asked…

“If someone proved this belief false tomorrow…

what evidence would convince you?”

(Rudhika blinked.)

Professor Vinay: I opened my mouth…

and realized I had no answer.

(The memory still seemed vivid to him.)

Professor Vinay: Then he asked another question.

“What evidence would make you change your mind?”

I couldn’t answer that either.

Because the truth was…

I wasn’t searching for truth.

I was searching for confirmation.

(Rudhika slowly repeated the sentence to herself.)

Rudhika: Confirmation…

Professor Vinay: Yes.

I wasn’t asking,

“Is this true?”

I was asking,

“How can I prove I’m already right?”

There’s a world of difference between those two questions.

(A breeze carried a few dry leaves across the pathway.)

Rudhika wrote the sentence carefully in her notebook.

Then she looked up.

Rudhika: Professor…

how do we know which one we’re searching for?

Truth…

or confirmation?

(Vinay nodded with approval.)

Professor Vinay: That’s a beautiful question.

In fact…

it’s one every thinker should ask themselves regularly.

(He picked up a fallen leaf from the ground.)

It was small.

Fresh.

Bright green.

He held it between his fingers.

Professor Vinay: Suppose I tell you…

this leaf is blue.

(Rudhika laughed.)

Rudhika: But it isn’t.

Professor Vinay: How do you know?

Rudhika: Because I can see it.

Professor Vinay: Good.

Should you believe me simply because I’m your professor?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Should you reject what I say simply because I happen to be wrong this time?

Rudhika: No…

Professor Vinay: Then what should you do?

(Rudhika looked at the leaf again.)

A smile slowly appeared on her face.

Rudhika: Look at the leaf.

Not at the person holding it.

(Vinay’s smile widened.)

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Truth doesn’t belong to professors.

It doesn’t belong to famous people.

It doesn’t belong to traditions.

It doesn’t belong to you.

It belongs only to reality.

Our job…

is to keep adjusting our beliefs until they match reality as closely as possible.

Not the other way around.

(Rudhika stared at the leaf for a long moment.)

Something about such a simple example made the idea feel surprisingly profound.

Rudhika: Then…

if someone wants to help another person discover the truth…

how should they do it?

Should they point out the mistake directly?

Or stay silent?

(Vinay gently placed the leaf back on the grass.)

Professor Vinay: Ah…

Now you’ve asked the question most people get wrong.

(Rudhika tilted her head.)

Professor Vinay: Tell me…

have you ever changed your opinion because someone shouted at you?

Rudhika: (Laughing softly.) Never.

Professor Vinay: Have you ever changed your mind because someone mocked you?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Neither have I.

Very few people have.

People rarely open their minds…

while they’re busy protecting their pride.

(The afternoon breeze fell still.)

Professor Vinay: If your goal is to defeat someone…

you may win the argument.

If your goal is to help someone see more clearly…

then making them feel respected is far more important than making them feel defeated.

(Rudhika closed her notebook.)

She wasn’t writing anymore.

She was simply listening.

Professor Vinay: Never begin with,

“You’re wrong.”

Begin with,

“Help me understand how you reached that conclusion.”

Because the moment people feel understood…

they become far more willing to understand you.

(Rudhika smiled.)

Rudhika: So…

the first step to changing someone’s mind…

isn’t speaking.

It’s listening.

(Vinay looked at her with quiet satisfaction.)

Professor Vinay: Precisely.

And that…

is where the search for truth truly begins.

(Rudhika remained silent for a few moments.

Her fingers traced absentmindedly over the edge of her notebook.

She looked thoughtful…

but not entirely convinced.)

Rudhika: Professor…

may I disagree with you?

(Vinay looked at her and smiled.)

Professor Vinay: I was beginning to worry you wouldn’t.

(Rudhika laughed.)

The nervousness she usually carried around him had begun to fade.

Rudhika: You said we should begin by understanding people…

listening to them…

respecting them.

But…

what if they’re obviously wrong?

What if they’re spreading something completely false?

Shouldn’t we correct them immediately?

(Vinay folded his arms.)

Instead of answering…

he asked another question.

Professor Vinay: Tell me…

have you ever tried pushing a door…

that says “Pull”?

(Rudhika looked confused.)

Rudhika: Yes.

Professor Vinay: What happened?

Rudhika: Nothing.

Professor Vinay: Did pushing harder help?

(Rudhika smiled.)

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Why not?

Rudhika: Because…

I was using the wrong approach.

(Vinay nodded.)

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Many people treat conversations the same way.

The harder the other person resists…

the harder they push.

Louder voice.

Stronger words.

More evidence.

More accusations.

And then they wonder why nothing changes.

(Rudhika thought back to the arguments she had observed the whole day.)

Professor Vinay: Winning an argument…

and opening a mind…

are often two very different skills.

(A pair of butterflies drifted across the garden, landing briefly on a flowering bush before fluttering away.)

Rudhika: So if facts aren’t enough…

what is?

(Vinay picked up a small pebble from the ground.)

He placed it gently in Rudhika’s palm.

Professor Vinay: Hold this.

(She looked at the pebble curiously.)

Professor Vinay: Imagine this pebble is one of your beliefs.

Close your hand.

(Rudhika closed her fingers around it.)

Professor Vinay: Tighter.

(She squeezed.)

Professor Vinay: Now imagine I try to take it from you by force.

What would you do?

Rudhika: I’d hold it tighter.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

The more force I use…

the tighter you grip.

(He paused.)

Professor Vinay: Now imagine instead…

I simply ask,

“Would you mind showing me the pebble?”

Would your hand still be as tight?

(Rudhika slowly relaxed her fingers.)

She opened her hand without even realizing she had done so.

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: That’s the difference between force…

and curiosity.

Force closes the hand.

Curiosity opens it.

(Rudhika stared at the pebble resting quietly in her palm.)

Something so ordinary…

had suddenly become unforgettable.

Rudhika: (Softly.)

So people don’t cling to beliefs…

because the beliefs are always strong.

Sometimes…

they cling because someone is trying to snatch them away.

(Vinay’s eyes lit up.)

He didn’t say “Correct.”

He simply nodded.

The best answers, he believed, were the ones students discovered themselves.

(A comfortable silence settled between them.)

Then, after a minute, Rudhika asked quietly,

Rudhika: Professor…

have you ever failed?

I mean…

have you ever tried to help someone understand…

and completely failed?

(Vinay looked toward the horizon.

His smile faded not into sadness…

but into reflection.)

Professor Vinay: More times than I can count.

And every one of those failures taught me something…

about human nature.

(Rudhika leaned forward.)

(Vinay took a slow breath.)

Professor Vinay: Let me tell you about the hardest conversation I’ve ever had…

(Vinay looked down at the pebble that still rested in Rudhika’s hand.)

Professor Vinay: This happened several years ago.

One of my closest friends believed something that simply wasn’t true.

I had evidence.

Research papers.

Experts.

Examples.

I thought changing his mind would be easy.

(Rudhika listened without interrupting.)

Professor Vinay: We sat together one evening for almost three hours.

I explained everything carefully.

Whenever he raised a point…

I answered it.

Whenever he doubted something…

I found another source.

By the time we finished…

I was convinced I had presented an airtight case.

Rudhika: Did he change his mind?

(Vinay smiled weakly.)

Professor Vinay: Not at all.

In fact…

he became even more certain that he was right.

(Rudhika looked surprised.)

Rudhika: But… why?

You had evidence.

Professor Vinay: I had something more dangerous than evidence.

Rudhika: What?

Professor Vinay: The desire to win.

(The words caught Rudhika off guard.)

Professor Vinay: I wasn’t trying to understand him anymore.

I was trying to defeat his arguments.

Every answer I gave made him feel cornered.

Every piece of evidence sounded like another attack.

He stopped listening.

Not because the evidence was weak…

but because he no longer felt safe enough to consider it.

(Rudhika looked down thoughtfully.)

Professor Vinay: We didn’t speak for several weeks after that conversation.

Not because either of us hated the other.

Because neither of us felt heard.

(A quiet silence settled over the garden.)

A squirrel darted across the path, disappearing into the roots of the banyan tree.

Rudhika: Did you ever talk about it again?

Professor Vinay: Yes.

Months later.

But something was different.

Rudhika: What changed?

Professor Vinay: Me.

(Rudhika looked up.)

Professor Vinay: The second time we met…

I made a promise to myself.

I wouldn’t mention a single piece of evidence for the first half hour.

Rudhika blinked.

Rudhika: Then… what did you talk about?

Professor Vinay: Him.

His experiences.

His reasons.

His fears.

His questions.

I wanted to understand not only what he believed…

but why he believed it.

Rudhika: And?

Professor Vinay: I discovered something I had completely missed the first time.

His belief wasn’t built on facts.

It was built on an experience from his childhood.

As long as I kept attacking the belief…

I was unknowingly attacking a memory that meant a great deal to him.

(Rudhika slowly nodded.)

Professor Vinay: That’s when I realized something.

Facts explain what people think.

Stories often explain why.

If you ignore the story…

the facts rarely find a place to stay.

(Rudhika wrote that sentence carefully in her notebook.)

She underlined it twice.

Then she closed the notebook.

Rudhika: Professor…

does that mean emotions are more important than facts?

(Vinay chuckled.)

Professor Vinay: No.

Facts help us discover reality.

Emotions help us understand people.

If you neglect either one…

your conversation becomes incomplete.

(He stood from the bench and brushed a few leaves from his trousers.)

Professor Vinay: Truth is discovered with the mind.

But it is often reached through the heart.

(Rudhika quietly repeated the sentence to herself.)

It was the kind of thought she knew she would remember long after today’s conversation ended.

End of Chapter 2

When Words Become Weapons

(The next morning, the college campus buzzed with its usual energy.

Students hurried between lectures.

Some laughed with friends.

Others rushed toward classrooms, hoping they weren’t late.

As Rudhika walked down the main corridor carrying her psychology notebook, raised voices caught her attention.)

A small crowd had gathered nearby.

Two students stood face to face.

One tried to explain something.

The other wasn’t listening.

Instead…

he laughed.

“Oh, so now you’re pretending to be an expert?”

Several students around them chuckled.

The first student’s face reddened.

He tried to speak again.

Before he could finish…

the other interrupted.

“Stop embarrassing yourself.”

More laughter.

(The conversation ended before it ever had a chance to begin.)

The first student quietly picked up his notebook and walked away.

The crowd slowly dispersed.

No one seemed particularly affected.

Except Rudhika.

(She stood there for several seconds.)

She hadn’t been the one insulted.

Yet something about the scene made her uncomfortable.

It wasn’t disagreement.

It wasn’t criticism.

It was the enjoyment of humiliating another person.

(The incident stayed in her mind throughout the day.)

When Professor Vinay’s psychology lecture ended, she waited as she always did until the other students had left.

(Vinay noticed the thoughtful expression on her face before she spoke.)

Professor Vinay: That’s the same expression you had after yesterday’s class.

Rudhika: (Smiling faintly.) Is it that obvious?

Professor Vinay: I’m a psychology professor.

Noticing things is part of the job.

(Rudhika laughed softly, but the smile quickly faded.)

They stepped into the corridor.

For a few moments, neither of them spoke.

Finally…

Rudhika broke the silence.

Rudhika: Professor…

Yesterday we talked about people who genuinely believe they’re right.

People who defend their beliefs because they think they’re protecting the truth.

(Vinay nodded.)

Rudhika stopped walking.

Rudhika: But what about people…

who don’t seem interested in truth at all?

People who interrupt…

mock…

insult…

or humiliate others…

not because they’re searching for understanding…

but simply because they enjoy hurting people.

(She looked directly at him.)

Rudhika: How do we deal with people who don’t respect us enough to even have an honest conversation?

(Vinay remained silent for a few moments.

He didn’t seem surprised by the question.

Instead…

he looked at the empty corridor stretching ahead of them.)

Professor Vinay: Before I answer…

tell me something.

When that student was being insulted this morning…

who did you feel sorry for?

(Rudhika answered without hesitation.)

Rudhika: The student who was being mocked.

Professor Vinay: Naturally.

And what did you feel toward the other student?

Rudhika: Honestly?

Professor Vinay: Always.

Rudhika: I was angry.

He wasn’t even trying to understand.

He just wanted everyone to laugh.

(Vinay nodded.)

Professor Vinay: That’s a very human reaction.

But let me ask you another question.

Who controlled your emotions today?

(Rudhika frowned.)

Rudhika: What do you mean?

Professor Vinay: You weren’t part of the argument.

Yet someone else’s behavior occupied your thoughts for hours.

(Rudhika became quiet.)

Professor Vinay: Think carefully.

Who decided how you would feel today?

The student…

or you?

(Rudhika looked down.)

She wanted to say, “I did.”

But it didn’t feel completely true.

(Vinay noticed her hesitation.)

Professor Vinay: Most people believe insults hurt because of the words themselves.

But words are only sounds…

until our minds give them meaning.

(Rudhika looked up.)

Rudhika: But Professor…

some words do hurt.

Professor Vinay: They do.

I’m not denying that.

I’m asking…

why they hurt.

(The question lingered.)

(Vinay bent down and picked up a dry twig from the ground.

He held it out toward Rudhika.)

Professor Vinay: If I call this twig…

a diamond…

does it become one?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Why not?

Rudhika: Because calling something by another name doesn’t change what it is.

(Vinay smiled.)

Then he gently pointed the twig toward her.

Professor Vinay: Suppose I call you…

“worthless.”

Does that sentence change who you are?

(Rudhika instinctively shook her head.)

Rudhika: No…

Professor Vinay: Does it change your abilities?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Your character?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Your kindness?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Then what has actually changed?

(Rudhika remained silent.)

Professor Vinay: Only this…

Someone has expressed an opinion.

Nothing more.

Nothing less.

(Rudhika wasn’t fully convinced.)

Rudhika: But if it’s only an opinion…

why does it feel so real?

(Vinay’s expression softened.)

Professor Vinay: Because we’re social beings.

From childhood…

our brains learn to care deeply about how others see us.

Acceptance once meant survival.

Rejection once meant danger.

Even today…

a harsh insult can awaken emotions that are thousands of years older than civilization itself.

So if insults affect you…

it doesn’t mean you’re weak.

It means you’re human.

(Rudhika let out a slow breath.)

For some reason…

hearing that made her feel lighter.

Professor Vinay: But being human…

doesn’t mean remaining helpless.

That’s where wisdom begins.

(Rudhika looked at him with renewed curiosity.)

Rudhika: Then…

how do we become wiser than our first reaction?

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: By asking one question before reacting.

Just one.

(Rudhika waited.)

Professor Vinay: “Is this person trying to help me…

or merely trying to hurt me?”

Because those are two very different conversations.

And they deserve two very different responses.

(Rudhika walked quietly beside Professor Vinay.

Students passed by them in both directions, but neither of them seemed to notice.

Her mind was entirely occupied by one thought.)

Rudhika: Professor…

how do I know which one it is?

Whether someone is trying to help me…

or simply trying to hurt me?

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: Excellent.

That’s exactly the question you should ask.

Not…

“Does this hurt?”

But…

“What is this person’s intention?”

(Rudhika nodded slowly.)

Professor Vinay: Let me give you a simple test.

Imagine two different people say exactly the same sentence to you.

“Your presentation wasn’t very clear.”

Should you react the same way to both?

Rudhika: I suppose… yes?

Professor Vinay: Let’s see.

Imagine the first person is your closest friend.

After everyone leaves, they quietly tell you,

“I know you worked hard.

I just think you explained the second topic too quickly.”

Why did they wait until everyone left?

Rudhika: Because they didn’t want to embarrass me.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Now imagine another student says the same thing.

But this time…

they say it loudly in front of the whole class.

Then they laugh.

Did the words change?

(Rudhika thought for a moment.)

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Then what changed?

Rudhika: The intention.

Professor Vinay: Precisely.

One person wanted to improve you.

The other wanted to display you.

One corrected.

The other humiliated.

Never confuse the two.

(Rudhika wrote another sentence in her notebook.)

“Judge criticism by its intention, not only by its words.”

(Vinay glanced at the page.)

Professor Vinay: That’s a good sentence.

But let’s make it even better.

(Rudhika looked up.)

Professor Vinay: Sometimes…

even a person with good intentions can be mistaken.

And sometimes…

a rude person accidentally speaks the truth.

(Rudhika blinked.)

Rudhika: I never thought of that.

Professor Vinay: That’s why wise people ask two separate questions.

First…

“Is it true?”

Second…

“How was it said?”

Never reverse the order.

(Rudhika frowned.)

Rudhika: Why?

(Vinay stopped walking.)

He looked at the flowerbed beside the pathway.

A rose bush grew there.

Beautiful flowers.

Sharp thorns.

He gently pointed toward it.

Professor Vinay: Tell me…

would you refuse a rose…

simply because it has thorns?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Would you grab the thorns…

because they’re attached to a rose?

(Rudhika laughed.)

Rudhika: Of course not.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Take the flower.

Leave the thorns.

If criticism contains truth…

keep the truth.

Leave the cruelty behind.

If it contains only cruelty…

there’s nothing to carry home.

(Rudhika smiled.)

She looked at the rose bush differently now.

Professor Vinay: The mistake many people make…

is carrying the thorns for years…

while leaving the flower behind.

(A gentle breeze carried the fragrance of the roses through the garden.)

For a few moments…

neither of them spoke.

Then Rudhika asked quietly,

Rudhika: Professor…

what if the person insulting me is someone I love?

A friend…

a parent…

or someone whose opinion matters to me?

Doesn’t that make it much harder?

(Vinay’s expression grew thoughtful.)

He nodded slowly.

Professor Vinay: Yes.

Much harder.

Because strangers can insult your ears.

But people you love…

can reach your heart.

(He looked at Rudhika with unusual seriousness.)

Professor Vinay: And that’s where psychology alone isn’t enough.

That conversation requires compassion…

boundaries…

and sometimes…

forgiveness.

(Rudhika sensed that this answer came not from a textbook…

but from experience.)

She closed her notebook.

She knew today’s lesson was far from over.

(The afternoon sun had begun its slow descent.

Long shadows stretched across the garden paths.)

(Rudhika walked in silence.

She replayed every sentence Professor Vinay had spoken.

She understood them.

At least…

she thought she did.

Yet one question refused to leave her mind.)

Rudhika: Professor…

may I be honest?

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: I would be disappointed if you weren’t.

(Rudhika took a slow breath.)

Rudhika: I understand everything you’ve said.

I really do.

But…

it still hurts.

Even when I know someone is wrong.

Even when I know they’re only trying to insult me…

it still hurts.

Why?

(Vinay’s smile faded into a thoughtful expression.)

For several seconds…

he didn’t answer.

Instead, he looked toward the horizon where the golden sunlight filtered through the trees.

Professor Vinay: Rudhika…

have you ever fallen while learning to ride a bicycle?

Rudhika: (Surprised.)

Many times.

Professor Vinay: Did knowing it was only a fall…

stop your knees from hurting?

(Rudhika smiled.)

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Understanding pain…

doesn’t erase pain.

It simply helps you respond to it more wisely.

(Rudhika listened carefully.)

Professor Vinay: Psychology is often misunderstood.

People think it teaches us how to stop feeling.

It doesn’t.

It teaches us how not to become prisoners of our feelings.

(The sentence lingered.)

Rudhika: So…

feeling hurt isn’t failure?

Professor Vinay: Not at all.

Feeling is automatic.

What you do next…

is your choice.

(A young boy chased a football across the college ground nearby.

He stumbled…

fell…

and immediately looked around.)

Rudhika noticed something.

The boy wasn’t checking his scraped knee.

He was checking whether anyone had seen him fall.

She smiled.

(Vinay noticed.)

Professor Vinay: What did you just observe?

Rudhika: He didn’t care about the injury first.

He cared about being embarrassed.

(Vinay nodded.)

Professor Vinay: That’s a psychologist’s observation.

(Rudhika couldn’t hide her smile.)

Professor Vinay: Sometimes…

the wound isn’t nearly as painful…

as the story we tell ourselves about the wound.

(Rudhika repeated the sentence softly.)

“The story we tell ourselves…”

Professor Vinay: Imagine two people hear exactly the same insult.

One thinks,

“Maybe they’re right.

I’m worthless.”

The other thinks,

“That was unkind.

I wonder why they’re so angry.”

Same words.

Different stories.

Different suffering.

(Rudhika slowed her pace.)

She had never separated the insult…

from the story that followed it.

Professor Vinay: We rarely suffer only because of what happened.

We also suffer because of the meaning we attach to what happened.

(Rudhika stopped walking.)

Rudhika: Then…

is changing the story…

the same as lying to ourselves?

(Vinay smiled.)

A pleased smile.

Not because the question was easy.

But because it was exactly the right question.

Professor Vinay: No.

Lying ignores reality.

Wisdom looks at reality…

without adding unnecessary suffering.

If someone insults you…

the reality is,

“They insulted me.”

The unnecessary story is,

“Therefore, I have no value.”

Those are not the same sentence.

(Rudhika looked down.

She realized how often she had unknowingly joined those two sentences together.)

The breeze gently turned a page of her notebook.

On the page were all the lessons she had written over the last two days.

Questions.

Observations.

Ideas.

She smiled quietly.

Perhaps…

she wasn’t only learning psychology anymore.

Perhaps…

she was learning how to understand herself.

(Vinay noticed the thoughtful look on Rudhika’s face.

He slowed his pace.)

Professor Vinay: There’s something else you should know.

(Rudhika looked up.)

Professor Vinay: The same words can affect two people very differently.

One person hears an insult…

shrugs…

and moves on.

Another carries those same words for years.

Rudhika: Why?

Professor Vinay: Because pain isn’t measured only by what is said.

It’s also shaped by who we are…

how we were raised…

what we’ve experienced…

what we’ve lost…

and what we’ve learned to believe about ourselves.

(Rudhika listened quietly.)

Professor Vinay: Psychology can explain a great deal about human behavior.

But no theory can completely explain a person.

Every individual carries a different story.

Different memories.

Different wounds.

Different strengths.

That’s why understanding someone begins long before giving them advice.

(Rudhika lowered her eyes.

His words felt strangely personal.)

Professor Vinay: Which is why…

I don’t think our next conversation should be about “people.”

I think…

it should be about you.

(Rudhika looked up almost immediately.)

Rudhika: M-me?

(Vinay smiled gently.)

Professor Vinay: Yes.

You’ve spent the last few days trying to understand the human mind.

Tomorrow…

if you’re comfortable with it…

I’d like to understand yours.

(Rudhika didn’t know what to say.)

For a brief moment, the world around her seemed unusually quiet.

Students walked past them.

A bicycle bell rang in the distance.

Someone called out to a friend across the courtyard.

Yet all of it faded into the background.

No one had ever asked to understand her before.

People had asked about her grades.

Her attendance.

Her assignments.

Her future.

But never…

her.

(A faint warmth spread across her cheeks.)

She quickly looked away, pretending to adjust the strap of her bag.

Rudhika: (Softly.) I… I don’t know if my story is interesting.

Professor Vinay: (With a kind smile.) Every mind is interesting.

The question is whether someone is patient enough to listen.

(Rudhika felt an unfamiliar feeling.

It wasn’t embarrassment alone.

It was relief.)

(Vinay glanced at his watch.)

Professor Vinay: It’s getting late.

Let’s continue tomorrow.

No theories.

No textbooks.

Just a conversation.

(Rudhika nodded.)

This time, her smile came effortlessly.

(As Professor Vinay walked toward the faculty building, Rudhika remained where she was for a few moments.

The garden was beginning to empty.

She looked down at her notebook.

For the first time since buying it…

she wondered whether the next page would contain lessons from a professor…

or pieces of her own life.

She gently closed the notebook and walked toward the college gate.

Tomorrow no longer felt like another class.

It felt like the beginning of being understood.)

End of Chapter 3

The Walls We Build

(The following afternoon, the college campus was quieter than usual.

Clouds drifted lazily across the sky, casting moving shadows over the garden where Professor Vinay and Rudhika had met every day that week.

For the first time…

neither of them carried a psychology textbook.

Only Rudhika held a small notebook against her chest.)

(Vinay was already sitting on the wooden bench beneath the banyan tree.

When he saw Rudhika approaching, he smiled.)

Professor Vinay: Right on time.

(Rudhika smiled faintly as she sat beside him.)

For a while…

neither of them spoke.

There was no awkwardness.

Only silence.

The kind of silence that exists between two people who don’t feel the need to fill every moment with words.

A cool breeze stirred the leaves overhead.

Somewhere nearby, a wind chime hanging outside the horticulture department rang softly.

Finally…

Vinay spoke.

Professor Vinay: Yesterday I promised that today wouldn’t be about theories.

It would be about you.

(Rudhika nodded.)

She looked down at her notebook.

Its pages were filled with observations from the previous days.

Yet today…

she hadn’t written a single word.

Professor Vinay: May I ask you something?

Rudhika: (Looking up.) Of course.

Professor Vinay: Why do you always sit alone after class?

(Rudhika blinked.)

She hadn’t expected that question.

Rudhika: I…

I don’t know.

Professor Vinay: Really?

Or have you simply never thought about it?

(Rudhika remained quiet.)

She searched for an answer.

At first…

nothing came.

Then…

small memories began surfacing.

Eating lunch alone.

Watching other students from a distance.

Leaving class before anyone could start a conversation.

Politely declining invitations.

Always choosing the corner seat.

Always.

Rudhika: (Softly.)

I guess…

it’s become a habit.

Professor Vinay: Habits usually have beginnings.

(Rudhika looked away.)

(Vinay didn’t continue.

He simply waited.

The silence wasn’t uncomfortable.

It was patient.)

After nearly a minute…

Rudhika finally spoke.

Rudhika: Professor…

have you ever noticed how some stray dogs behave?

(Vinay looked at her with curiosity.)

Rudhika: If they’ve always been loved…

they’ll happily run toward anyone.

But if they’ve been beaten over and over again…

even someone trying to feed them has to earn their trust.

(Vinay didn’t interrupt.)

(Rudhika gave a small, almost embarrassed smile.)

Rudhika: I think…

people can become like that too.

(Those words seemed to surprise even her.

She had never described herself that way before.)

Professor Vinay: That’s a thoughtful observation.

Do you think you’ve stopped trusting people…

or have you stopped expecting kindness from them?

(Rudhika felt the question settle somewhere deep inside her.)

She wanted to answer immediately.

But she couldn’t.

Because she wasn’t sure.

For several moments…

she simply stared at the grass beneath her feet.

Then…

very quietly…

she spoke.

Rudhika: Professor…

I never really knew my parents.

(Vinay’s expression softened.

He didn’t say he was sorry.

He didn’t interrupt.

He simply listened.)

Rudhika: They died in an accident when I was still a toddler.

I don’t remember their faces.

I don’t remember their voices.

Sometimes…

I wonder what it would have felt like…

to remember being hugged by them.

(The words came slowly.

As if they had been waiting years to be spoken.)

Rudhika: My elder sister raised me.

She was still a child herself.

But somehow…

she became everything.

She wasn’t just my sister.

She became my family.

(She smiled faintly.)

Everything gentle in my life…

came from her.

(The smile slowly disappeared.)

Rudhika: We lived with our grandparents.

People always say grandparents spoil their grandchildren.

(Oddly…

that sentence made Rudhika laugh.

But there was no joy in it.)

Rudhika: That wasn’t our story.

(Vinay remained completely still.

He could sense that what came next carried years of silence.)

(Rudhika took a slow, trembling breath.)

She looked at the empty page of her notebook.

Rudhika: There was one day…

when I learned…

that sometimes the people who are supposed to protect you…

can become the people you’re most afraid of.

(She closed the notebook.)

Her fingers trembled ever so slightly.

(Vinay noticed.

He didn’t ask her to continue.

He didn’t tell her to “be strong.”

He simply said,)

Professor Vinay: We have all the time you need.

(Rudhika looked at him.

For the first time in years…

she believed him.)

She drew another slow breath.

Then…

she began.

(Rudhika looked at the notebook resting in her hands.

She slowly traced a finger along its blank page.

When she finally spoke…

her voice was barely above a whisper.)

Rudhika: I think…

I should start with him.

Our cousin.

(For a brief moment, she wondered if she should even continue.

Then she remembered Professor Vinay’s words.

“We have all the time you need.”

She took another breath.)

Rudhika: My sister and I lived with our grandparents after our parents died.

There was also our cousin.

He was around my age.

Maybe a little older.

Everyone adored him.

Whatever he did…

someone had an excuse for it.

If my sister or I made a mistake…

it became a crime.

(Vinay listened without interrupting.)

Rudhika: When I was little…

I didn’t understand favoritism.

I just thought…

maybe I wasn’t trying hard enough.

Maybe if I behaved better…

they would love me too.

(She gave a quiet laugh.)

Children are strange.

They always think they are responsible for the weather inside a house.

(Vinay made a mental note of the sentence but didn’t stop her.)

Rudhika: One afternoon…

my grandparents had gone out.

My sister wasn’t home.

It was just me…

and him.

She had asked me to fold the freshly washed clothes.

I was happy to do it.

I wanted everything to be neat before they returned.

(She smiled faintly.)

I folded every piece carefully.

One by one.

I still remember checking each shirt twice…

because I didn’t want anyone to complain.

(Her smile disappeared.)

Then…

without saying a word…

he picked up the pile of clothes…

and threw them over the balcony.

(The memory seemed to return with startling clarity.)

Rudhika stared at the ground.

Almost as though she were seeing the scattered clothes again.

Rudhika: I panicked.

I ran downstairs as fast as I could.

Some clothes had fallen into the dust.

Some were tangled in the plants.

I picked up every single one.

I dusted them with my hands.

I thought…

if I hurried…

maybe no one would know.

(She swallowed.)

When I came back upstairs…

he was waiting.

(For the first time since beginning her story…

her hands started trembling.)

Rudhika: He smiled.

Not because he was happy.

Because he knew something I didn’t.

He stood in front of me and said…

“Good girl.

Now hand them to me again.”

(Vinay remained silent.)

Rudhika: I begged him not to.

I told him Grandmother would be angry.

I told him we’d both get into trouble.

He only laughed.

Every time I pulled the clothes back…

he pulled harder.

Like it was a game.

Like my fear was entertaining.

(Her breathing became slower.)

Rudhika: I don’t even remember deciding to do it.

My hand just…

moved.

I slapped him.

(The words hung in the air.)

Rudhika: It wasn’t because I hated him.

It was because…

for one second…

I wanted the game to stop.

(She closed her eyes.)

Instead…

everything became worse.

He slapped me back immediately.

I remember it felt like my neck bend.

I remember falling.

I remember the ceiling spinning.

And then…

I remember lying on the floor.

Crying.

Not because of the slap.

Because I already knew…

what was going to happen next.

(Vinay’s expression changed ever so slightly.)

He wasn’t shocked.

He was listening with complete attention.

Rudhika continued.

Rudhika: A little while later…

my grandparents came home.

The clothes were still dirty.

I just get up from the floor.

He reached them before I could say a single word.

He told them I had thrown the clothes myself.

He told them I had hit him for no reason.

(She paused.)

I tried to explain.

I really tried.

But no one asked me what happened.

No one looked at me.

Their minds had already decided.

(The garden had become remarkably quiet.)

Even the sounds of students in the distance seemed to fade.

Rudhika looked down at her hands.

They had stopped trembling.

Not because the memory hurt less.

But because she had finally spoken it aloud.

Rudhika: That day…

their were already angry because of something...

they beat me so much that I thought I will gonna die.

My sister came between me and them.

She covered me with her own body and got beaten too.

If she hadn’t…

I don’t know what would have happened.

(Silence.)

A long silence.

Not empty.

Respectful.

Professor Vinay did not rush to comfort her.

He knew that some stories should be honored before they are answered.

Rudhika looked toward the old banyan tree.

For years…

she had carried this memory alone.

Today…

for the first time…

someone had listened without judging.

And somehow…

that changed the memory just a little.

(The breeze carried a few dry leaves across the stone pathway.

Neither of them spoke.

Several minutes passed.

Professor Vinay didn’t seem interested in filling the silence.

He simply remained there.

Present.

Listening.)

(Rudhika wiped the corner of one eye before the tear could fall.)

Rudhika: I was fourteen.

Old enough to know what was happening.

Old enough to remember every second of it.

(She let out a quiet laugh.)

Sometimes people think painful memories disappear with time.

Mine became clearer.

(Vinay nodded gently.)

Professor Vinay: Memories tied to strong emotions often do.

Especially the ones our minds believe are important for survival.

(Rudhika looked toward the ground.)

Rudhika: After that…

I changed.

I stopped arguing.

I stopped explaining.

Whenever someone blamed me…

I just stayed quiet.

Because…

what was the point?

No one had listened that day.

Why would anyone listen later?

(Vinay listened carefully.)

Rudhika: I stopped trusting compliments too.

If someone was kind…

I kept waiting for them to become cruel.

If someone smiled…

I wondered what they wanted.

It felt…

safer to expect the worst.

(She looked embarrassed.)

Rudhika: That’s probably why I stay away from people now.

It’s easier to be alone.

If you don’t let anyone close…

they can’t hurt you.

(Professor Vinay folded his hands in his lap.)

He remained thoughtful for a moment.

Then he asked quietly,

Professor Vinay: May I ask you something?

Rudhika: Of course.

Professor Vinay: Imagine a fourteen-year-old girl came to my office tomorrow.

She sat exactly where you’re sitting now.

And she told me the same story you just told me.

Every detail.

(He paused.)

Professor Vinay: Would you think she deserved what happened?

(Rudhika answered almost instantly.)

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Would you call her weak?

Rudhika: Never.

Professor Vinay: Would you tell her she should have known better?

Rudhika frowned.

Rudhika: No.

She was only trying to stop someone from tormenting her.

(Vinay nodded.)

Professor Vinay: Then let me ask one last question.

Why does that kindness disappear…

when the fourteen-year-old is you?

(Rudhika opened her mouth to answer.

Nothing came out.)

For the first time…

she realized there were two versions of compassion inside her.

One for everyone else.

And another…

far harsher one for herself.

(Vinay didn’t interrupt her thoughts.)

He knew some questions should echo before they’re answered.

After nearly a minute, Rudhika spoke.

Very softly.

Rudhika: Because…

if I admit I didn’t deserve it…

then I have to admit something even more frightening.

Professor Vinay: What is that?

(Her eyes filled again.)

Rudhika: That the people who were supposed to protect me…

chose not to.

(The words seemed to drain years of weight from her shoulders.)

Vinay didn’t rush to respond.

Instead, he looked up at the branches of the banyan tree.

Professor Vinay: When we cannot make sense of another person’s cruelty…

our minds often search for an explanation.

Especially when we’re young.

Children and teenagers have very little control over the adults around them.

So the mind reaches for the one thing it can control.

“Often it decides…”

(He looked back at Rudhika.)

“…‘It must be me.’

’If I were better…

quieter…

smarter…

more obedient…

maybe they would have loved me.’”

(Rudhika’s eyes widened.)

She had never spoken those thoughts aloud.

Yet somehow…

he had described them almost exactly.

Professor Vinay: Those conclusions can feel convincing.

Not because they’re true.

But because they give chaos a reason.

And a reason…

even a painful one…

can feel less frightening than believing the people around you acted unjustly.

(Rudhika sat quietly.

For years, she had believed that becoming invisible was wisdom.

Now, for the first time, she wondered whether it had simply been the safest way a frightened fourteen-year-old knew how to survive.)

The afternoon bell rang across the campus.

Neither of them moved.

Some conversations…

were more important than the timetable.

(The afternoon bell had long since faded.

The pathways that had been crowded an hour ago were now almost empty.

Only a few students remained scattered across the campus.)

(Rudhika leaned back against the bench.

She felt exhausted.

Not physically.

Emotionally.

As though she had been carrying a heavy box for years…

and had finally set it down.)

Neither of them spoke.

The silence no longer felt heavy.

It felt peaceful.

After several minutes, Professor Vinay spoke.

Professor Vinay: Thank you.

(Rudhika looked at him, surprised.)

Rudhika: For what?

Professor Vinay: For trusting me with your story.

Trust isn’t given because someone is a professor.

It’s given because someone feels safe.

I don’t take that lightly.

(Rudhika lowered her eyes.)

She wasn’t used to people thanking her for speaking.

Usually…

they thanked her for staying quiet.

Vinay continued.

Professor Vinay: May I share one observation?

Rudhika nodded.

Professor Vinay: Everything you’ve described…

your silence…

your hesitation…

your fear of getting close to people…

they all make sense.

Not because they’re ideal.

But because somewhere in your life…

they protected you.

(Rudhika listened carefully.)

Professor Vinay: Imagine you’re caught in a storm.

You build a small shelter to survive.

The shelter saves your life.

Years later…

the storm is over.

But you never leave.

What once protected you…

slowly becomes a prison.

(Rudhika looked toward the sky.)

The clouds had almost disappeared.

She smiled faintly.

Rudhika: So…

I’m still living inside the shelter.

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: Perhaps.

And perhaps that’s alright.

You don’t tear down a shelter overnight.

You first walk outside long enough to realize…

the storm isn’t always there anymore.

(Rudhika quietly absorbed the thought.)

For the first time…

she didn’t feel ashamed of the person she had become.

She saw a frightened fourteen-year-old…

doing her best to survive.

Maybe…

that girl deserved understanding…

not judgment.

A gentle breeze rustled the banyan leaves above them.

Rudhika watched them dance for a moment before speaking again.

Rudhika: Professor…

there’s something I still don’t understand.

(Vinay turned toward her.)

Rudhika: Why are people like that?

Why do some people enjoy hurting others?

Why are some homes filled with fear instead of love?

Why do people become so abusive?

Why do people hate someone simply because they’re different…

or because they belong to another religion…

another caste…

another country…

another group?

Why does identity become more important than humanity?

(She paused.)

Rudhika: Were my grandparents always like that?

Was my cousin born that way?

Or…

did something make them become those people?

(The questions lingered in the evening air.)

Professor Vinay didn’t answer immediately.

Instead, he looked across the campus where students from countless different backgrounds laughed together on the lawn.

Then he looked back at Rudhika.

A gentle smile crossed his face.

Professor Vinay: Those…

are some of the oldest questions in psychology.

And perhaps…

some of the oldest questions in human history.

(Rudhika waited.)

Professor Vinay: If I answer them in five minutes…

I’ll only give you opinions.

They deserve something better.

They deserve careful thought.

(He stood, picking up the book he had brought but never opened.)

Professor Vinay: Tomorrow…

we’ll begin exploring why people become who they become.

We’ll talk about childhood…

learning…

fear…

identity…

power…

love…

and hate.

Not to excuse cruelty.

But to understand it.

Because understanding why something exists…

is the first step toward knowing how to prevent it.

(Rudhika stood as well.)

For the first time since she had entered college…

she wasn’t looking forward to tomorrow because of a class.

She was looking forward to a conversation.

The sun slipped below the horizon.

Together…

they walked toward the college gate.

Not as a professor and his student.

But as two people…

trying to understand the human mind.

End of Chapter 4

Beyond Labels

(The next morning…

the campus seemed unaware of the questions waiting beneath the old banyan tree.

Students hurried to lectures.

Some complained about assignments.

Some laughed over yesterday’s jokes.

Life moved exactly as it always had.

Yet for Rudhika…

today felt different.

Today wasn’t about remembering her past.

It was about understanding humanity.)

(Professor Vinay was already seated on the familiar wooden bench.

A notebook rested beside him.

Not a psychology textbook.

Just blank pages.)

(Rudhika approached.)

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: Good morning.

Rudhika: Good morning, Professor.

(She sat beside him.)

Neither of them spoke immediately.

The breeze carried the scent of wet earth from last night’s rain.

Finally…

Vinay opened the notebook.

On the first page he had written only one sentence.

“To understand a person, first understand the forces that shaped them.”

He turned the notebook so Rudhika could read it.

Professor Vinay: Yesterday you asked me many difficult questions.

(Rudhika nodded.)

Professor Vinay: Do you remember them?

Rudhika smiled faintly.

Rudhika: Every one of them.

Professor Vinay: Good.

Then ask them again.

Sometimes…

important questions deserve to be heard twice.

(Rudhika looked toward the garden.)

She spoke slowly.

Almost exactly as she had the evening before.

Rudhika: Why are people like that?

Why do some people enjoy hurting others?

Why are some homes filled with fear instead of love?

Why do people become abusive?

Why do people hate others simply because they’re different…

because they belong to another religion…

another caste…

another country…

another community?

Why does identity become more important than humanity?

(She paused.)

Rudhika: Were my grandparents always like that?

Was my cousin born that way?

Or…

did something make them become those people?

(The questions settled quietly between them.)

Professor Vinay remained silent for several moments.

Not because he lacked an answer.

But because some answers deserve a moment of respect before they are spoken.

Finally…

he asked a question of his own.

Professor Vinay: Rudhika…

when you were born…

could you speak Marathi?

She smiled.

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Could you walk?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Could you hate someone because of their religion?

(Rudhika frowned.)

Rudhika: Of course not.

Professor Vinay: Why not?

(Rudhika thought.)

Rudhika: Because…

I didn’t know what religion was.

Vinay nodded.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

No child is born knowing caste.

Or politics.

Or nationality.

Or prejudice.

Those are learned.

Just as language is learned.

(Rudhika’s attention sharpened.)

Professor Vinay: Human beings are born with certain natural tendencies.

The need to survive.

The need to belong.

The ability to feel fear.

The ability to love.

The ability to learn.

But who we become…

is shaped by an ongoing conversation between our biology…

our experiences…

our family…

our friends…

our teachers…

our culture…

and the choices we make.

(Rudhika wrote quickly.)

Vinay continued.

Professor Vinay: Psychology has a simple saying.

“Genes load the gun.

Environment aims it.

Choice pulls or refuses to pull the trigger.”

(Rudhika looked up.)

Professor Vinay: That doesn’t mean people have no responsibility.

Many people endure terrible childhoods…

and still choose kindness.

Others grow up surrounded by love…

yet become cruel.

Our past influences us.

It does not imprison us.

(Rudhika underlined the sentence.)

Professor Vinay: Your grandparents…

your cousin…

I cannot tell you exactly why they became who they were.

No psychologist can do that without truly knowing them.

But we can understand some of the forces that often shape people.

Power.

Fear.

Humiliation.

Neglect.

Learned behavior.

Sometimes…

people who grow up in homes where shouting is normal…

begin to believe shouting is communication.

People who grow up seeing violence…

may mistake violence for authority.

Children learn far more from what adults do…

than from what adults say.

(Rudhika remembered countless moments from her childhood.)

Vinay noticed.

Professor Vinay: Tell me…

if a child grows up watching adults solve every disagreement with insults…

what do you think that child learns?

(Rudhika answered quietly.)

Rudhika: That insults are normal.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

If love is never demonstrated…

how will the child recognize healthy love later?

If every mistake is punished with humiliation…

how will that child respond when someone else makes a mistake?

(Rudhika slowly understood.)

Professor Vinay: This is one reason psychologists pay so much attention to childhood.

Not because childhood decides everything.

But because it often writes the first draft of our beliefs about the world.

(The breeze gently turned another page of the notebook.)

Vinay looked at the blank page.

Professor Vinay: But your questions didn’t end with abusive families.

They reached something even larger.

They reached humanity itself.

(Rudhika nodded.)

Professor Vinay: So let me ask you another question.

When you see students on this campus…

what do you notice first?

Their religion?

Their caste?

Their language?

Or simply…

that they are students?

(Rudhika looked across the lawn.

Hundreds of students.

Walking together.

Laughing together.

Arguing together.

Learning together.)

She remained silent.

Because she had already begun discovering the answer.

And Professor Vinay knew it.

(The morning sun climbed a little higher.

Students continued moving across the campus.

Some wore white lab coats.

Some carried cricket bats.

Some spoke in Marathi.

Others in Hindi, English, Tamil, Bengali, Punjabi, and dozens of other languages.

To most people…

it was simply another college day.

To Professor Vinay…

it was a living psychology laboratory.)

(Vinay looked toward the students.)

Professor Vinay: Rudhika…

do you know why humans create groups?

(Rudhika thought.)

Rudhika: Because we like people who are similar to us?

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: That’s part of it.

But let’s go much further back.

Thousands of years.

Imagine you’re living in a forest.

No cities.

No police.

No hospitals.

No supermarkets.

Only small groups of people trying to survive.

(Rudhika imagined the scene.)

Professor Vinay: If someone from your own group became ill…

would you help them?

Rudhika: Of course.

Professor Vinay: Why?

Rudhika: Because they’re my people.

Vinay nodded.

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Now imagine another group competing for the same water…

the same food…

the same land.

Your brain has to answer one question very quickly.

“Friend or danger?”

Sometimes…

answering incorrectly meant death.

(Rudhika slowly understood.)

Professor Vinay: The human brain became remarkably good at recognizing groups.

Not because groups are evil.

Because survival required cooperation.

Families.

Villages.

Tribes.

Communities.

Without them…

our ancestors probably wouldn’t have survived.

(Rudhika looked across the campus.)

Professor Vinay: So the desire to belong isn’t a flaw.

It’s deeply human.

Everyone wants to feel…

“I have people.”

No matter where they’re born.

No matter what language they speak.

(Vinay picked up two small twigs from the ground.)

He placed them separately on the bench.

Professor Vinay: Imagine this twig is you.

And this twig is another person.

Individually…

both are easy to break.

(He snapped one twig effortlessly.)

Then he picked up several more fallen twigs.

He tied them loosely together using a blade of grass.

He tried to bend them.

They resisted.

Professor Vinay: Groups gave human beings strength.

Protection.

Identity.

Purpose.

None of that is wrong.

(Rudhika nodded.)

Professor Vinay: But every strength carries a shadow.

(Rudhika looked up.)

Professor Vinay: The same mind that says,

“These are my people…”

can also begin saying,

“Those are not.”

And once someone becomes “not us”…

something dangerous can happen.

Empathy begins to shrink.

(Rudhika was listening intently.)

Professor Vinay: Tell me…

have you ever noticed that people sometimes say things about entire groups…

that they would never say to a person’s face?

(Rudhika thought for a moment.)

Then nodded.

Rudhika: Yes.

Someone might say…

“All people from that religion are like this.”

Or…

“Everyone from that country is selfish.”

But if they actually meet someone from that group…

they often behave differently.

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: Precisely.

Because labels are simple.

People are complicated.

The brain likes shortcuts.

Reality rarely cooperates.

(A few first-year students walked past them laughing loudly.

One accidentally dropped his notebook.

Without hesitation…

students from completely different departments stopped to help him gather the scattered pages.

Within seconds…

they continued walking in different directions.

None of them asked each other’s religion.

Or caste.

Or political opinions.

They simply saw…

someone who needed help.)

Vinay pointed toward them.

Professor Vinay: Did you notice what just happened?

(Rudhika smiled.)

Rudhika: They didn’t help a Hindu.

Or a Muslim.

Or a Maharashtrian.

Or an engineering student.

They helped…

a person.

(Vinay’s eyes brightened.)

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

Before every label…

there is a human being.

The problem begins when we forget the order.

First comes the person.

Then comes every identity they carry.

Never reverse them.

(Rudhika wrote the sentence carefully.)

“When identity comes before humanity…

compassion becomes conditional.”

(She looked at what she had written.)

Vinay nodded approvingly.

Professor Vinay: History has shown us something remarkable.

The greatest acts of kindness…

and the greatest acts of cruelty…

have both been committed by ordinary human beings.

Not monsters.

Not angels.

People.

(Rudhika frowned.)

Rudhika: Then…

if this tendency exists in everyone…

how do we prevent it?

(Vinay looked toward the ancient banyan tree.)

Its branches spread in every direction.

Birds of different colors rested on the same limbs.

Some stayed only for a moment.

Others built nests.

The tree rejected none of them.

A gentle smile appeared on his face.

Professor Vinay: More than two thousand years ago…

the sages of this land noticed the same tendency you’re asking about.

They saw how easily human beings divided themselves into “us” and “them.”

So they offered a different way of looking at the world.

Not as competing tribes…

but as one human family.

They expressed that vision in a simple Sanskrit phrase.

“वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम्” Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam.

(Rudhika had heard the phrase before.

But today…

she felt she was about to understand it for the first time.)

She closed her notebook.

Not because the lesson was ending.

But because she wanted to listen…

without writing a single word.

(The garden had grown quieter.

Even the usual chatter from nearby classrooms seemed distant.

Professor Vinay gently picked up a fallen banyan leaf.

He held it between his fingers for a moment before speaking.)

Professor Vinay: Rudhika…

what do you think people mean when they hear the phrase…

“Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam”?

Rudhika thought for a moment.

Rudhika: That…

the whole world is one family.

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: That’s the translation.

But translations rarely carry the entire idea.

(Rudhika waited.)

Professor Vinay: Tell me…

is every family peaceful?

(Rudhika laughed softly.)

Rudhika: Definitely not.

Professor Vinay: Do brothers always agree?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Do parents never make mistakes?

Rudhika: No.

Professor Vinay: Can family members hurt each other?

(The smile slowly disappeared from Rudhika’s face.)

She answered quietly.

Rudhika: Yes.

Sometimes…

very deeply.

(Vinay nodded.)

Professor Vinay: Then “the world is one family” cannot possibly mean…

“Everyone is always kind.”

Because even families struggle.

(The banyan leaf slipped gently from his hand and landed on the ground.)

Professor Vinay: The sages weren’t describing reality as it already existed.

They were describing a way of seeing.

An ideal to practice.

A reminder.

Before you are a Hindu…

a Muslim…

a Christian…

a Buddhist…

an atheist…

an Indian…

an American…

a scientist…

or a teacher…

you are first…

a human being.

And before that…

a living being capable of joy…

fear…

love…

and suffering.

(Rudhika listened carefully.)

Professor Vinay: Every newborn enters this world crying.

Not in Sanskrit.

Not in English.

Not in Arabic.

Not in Chinese.

Just…

crying.

Everyone laughs.

Everyone loses someone.

Everyone fears rejection.

Everyone searches for meaning.

The details differ.

The experience of being human…

is shared.

(Rudhika slowly closed her eyes.)

She remembered the pain she had carried for years.

Then she imagined…

perhaps countless others carried different pains…

just as invisible.

Vinay continued.

Professor Vinay: This idea doesn’t ask us to erase differences.

Differences are beautiful.

Languages.

Music.

Food.

Traditions.

Ways of celebrating.

Ways of praying.

Ways of thinking.

Human civilization would be poorer without them.

The problem begins…

when identity stops becoming something we have…

and starts becoming the only thing we are.

(Rudhika wrote carefully.)

“Identity should describe us.

It should never imprison us.”

(Vinay smiled.)

Professor Vinay: Exactly.

When identity becomes the center of our entire self…

every disagreement feels like a personal attack.

That’s why people become defensive so quickly.

They’re not protecting an idea.

They’re protecting the story they’ve built about themselves.

(Rudhika suddenly remembered their conversation from Chapter Two.)

She smiled.

Rudhika: You told me…

people often defend themselves…

not their beliefs.

Vinay smiled back.

Professor Vinay: I’m glad you remembered.

Psychology has a habit of connecting today’s lesson with yesterday’s.

(For a few moments they simply watched students crossing the campus.)

A young man wearing a cricket jersey greeted a girl wearing a laboratory coat.

Another student carrying a guitar opened the library door for an elderly professor.

Nearby…

someone offered water to a campus gardener working under the morning sun.

No one asked each other which community they belonged to before helping.

Humanity had quietly arrived before identity.

(Vinay pointed toward them.)

Professor Vinay: Notice something.

Goodness rarely announces its religion.

Kindness rarely introduces its caste.
